newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS - Kazakh gas trapped by Russian pipeline veto.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kazakh gas trapped by Russian pipeline veto.

text.p: Russia's jealous eye on Europe's natural gas market and its grip on export pipelines has stalled development of Kazakhstan's large Karachaganak gas field, Kazakh officials and analysts said on Friday.

Russia inherited control of the former Soviet Union's oil and gas pipeline network, making resource-rich but landlocked Central Asian states more or less beholden to Moscow for the transport of their energy exports.

"Karachaganak's main problem is exports -- this is why the project is not progressing," said Vyacheslav Nupov, vice-president of state-owned Kazakhgaz, the concern which represents Kazakhstan in the production-sharing deal.
Kazakhstan's $10 billion, 40-year Karachaganak project, which once included Gazprom, depends on getting the output from under the parched Kazakh steppe to Western markets.
Gazprom chief executive Rem Vyakhirev said on Thursday that he did not want Kazakh gas travelling through Russian export pipelines.
Anxious at competition posed by gas from Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan, Vyakhirev said: "To give up one's market...would be, at the very least, a crime before Russia."
Karachaganak, located near the republic's northwestern border with Russia, boasts 1.33 trillion cubic metres of natural gas, 644 million tonnes of gas condensate and 190 million tonnes of oil.
It is being developed by Texaco Inc, British Gas, Agip and Russia's LUKoil.
Karachaganak, which could produce at a peak rate of 20-22 billion cubic metres of natural gas annually, now pumps only a paltry four million cubic feet of gas daily.
"We are now focusing on possibilities in the Kazakh market," said one of Karachaganak's western members.
While Kazakhstan is looking to build gas-fired power stations to provide power for the republic's heavy industry, pressure continues to use coal to preserve jobs in mining.
Greater domestic power demand is unlikely to kick in for some time.
Stephen O'Sullivan, Director of Oil and Gas at MC Securities Ltd in London, said: "One of Gazprom's worries is pressure on prices in the European gas market".

"While demand in Europe is set to grow by 45 percent over the next 10-15 years, the number of suppliers are multiplying so why let a competitor like Karachaganak into your (pipeline) system?" he said.
The republic of 17 million, scattered over an area the size of western Europe, is also wondering what to do with large volumes of gas when other major oil projects come on stream.

The head of Kazakhstan's Agency for the Control of Natural Resources, Galymzhan Zhakiyanov, has urged the government to write Russia and Europe out of its long-term export plans and look to Asian markets instead.

In a report sent to Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev and given to Reuters on Friday, Zhakiyanov wrote: "The strong markets are in the southeast -- demand for oil and gas in China, Korea, Taiwan and Japan continues to rise".

An oil pipeline to China was mooted in June when the China National Petroleum Corp won the right to develop a substantial field while Nazarbayev has said he would like to see a pipeline built to export gas to its neighbour.
But a pipeline to China's main areas of demand, still thousands of kilometres (miles) away, would cost billions of dollars.
Other export options south are held up by fighting in Afghanistan and a politically charged investment climate in Iran.
--Almaty Newsroom, +7 3272 509410
